name: Hand, toe and body warmers
summary: Pocket heat: single-use air-activated iron-powder packs, reusable sodium-acetate click packs, lighter-fluid catalytic warmers and battery warmers. Hours of warmth for hands and feet; they burn skin held against them, and the fluid kind makes carbon monoxide.
uses: Hands and feet for hours: Grabber's hand warmer runs about 10 h at an average 57 °C (135 °F), its toe warmer about 8 h at an average 36 °C (97 °F) (Grabber hand, Grabber toe)

Warm hands and feet while you are awake, over clothing or gloves. Makers say warmers pressed against the body or worn while asleep cause low-temperature burns, and only a medical-device heat patch is meant for bare skin (MYCOAL FAQ)
Reusable sodium-acetate packs: 30 minutes to 2 hours of heat, recharged hundreds of times by boiling (HotSnapZ FAQ)
Lighter-fluid catalytic warmers: about 6 or 12 hours from one fill, depending on model and fill line (Zippo hand warmer)
Not a room heater and not a fix for hypothermia on its own: shelter, dry clothes, insulation and food come first
identify: Air-activated: a cloth pouch sealed in a plastic wrapper; the mix is iron powder, water, salt, activated charcoal and vermiculite (Kobayashi FAQ), and it heats when air reaches it (Ignik not working). HotHands-type products run about 38–82 °C (100–180 °F) for 1 to 18+ hours depending on type (Kobayashi FAQ). Toe warmers run cooler (Grabber toe: up to 46 °C, average 36 °C) than hand warmers (Grabber hand: up to 70 °C, average 57 °C). Body warmers are larger pads; follow the pack, and note that MYCOAL says only a medical-device heat patch is meant for bare skin (MYCOAL FAQ). Sodium-acetate packs: a clear liquid pouch with a small metal disc; flexing the disc turns it white, solid and hot (HotSnapZ FAQ). Catalytic warmers: a flat metal case with a cotton-filled fuel cup and a burner head, filled with lighter fluid and lit once, then heating without a flame inside a cloth bag (Zippo hand warmer, Zippo hand warmer guide). Battery warmers: rechargeable, with a lithium-ion battery and a charging cable; check the model and batch number against recalls (Health Canada OCOOPA, CPSC HotHands rechargeable).
test: Air-activated: a good unused pack feels soft and loose. A hard, lumpy one has had air through a torn wrapper and is spent (Ignik not working). Read the date: MYCOAL gives usually 4 years (MYCOAL FAQ), Grabber 2–3 years (Grabber home); past it, try one before you rely on the box. To start one, shake it and leave it open to the air for up to 15 minutes; frozen packs (they contain water) need warming first, and one smothered in a tight waterproof pocket may need more air (Ignik not working). Sodium acetate: clear and liquid means charged; white and hard means it needs boiling until every crystal has gone, plus a minute (HotSnapZ FAQ). A leaking pack is finished. Catalytic: the burner needs replacing after about 70 uses, the cloth bag must be there, and lighter fluid evaporates even from an unused warmer, so check the fuel (Zippo hand warmer guide). Battery warmers: stop using any that swell, hiss or get hotter than usual (see the swollen lithium cell guide). Both recalls say the lithium-ion battery can overheat and ignite, with risk of serious injury from fire and burns (CPSC HotHands rechargeable, Health Canada OCOOPA); CPSC reports no injuries.

decay.note: Estimate. Air-activated packs carry a 2–4 year date (Grabber home, MYCOAL FAQ) and die early if a wrapper tears. Sodium-acetate packs and catalytic cases last years; catalytic burners wear out with use.

improvise: A hot-water bottle, or a sealed bottle of hot (not boiling) water in a sock, does the same job; check it for leaks and close the cap tight (HK Consumer Council). Every one of these burns at the skin if held there: burns can happen at only about 43 °C with long contact (HK Consumer Council). Keep heat off people who can't feel it or move away: young children, older people and diabetics have reduced sensation (Kobayashi FAQ), and MYCOAL says infants, children, older people and disabled people who can't take a warmer off need someone watching them (MYCOAL FAQ). Keep air-activated pouches away from young children: the contents can be mistaken for drink powder and harm the mouth and gut if swallowed (HK Consumer Council). Never sleep with a warmer against you (MYCOAL FAQ). Catalytic warmers release carbon monoxide as well as carbon dioxide, and the council warns that in a confined space the CO can kill (HK Consumer Council): keep them out of sleeping bags, closed cars and small shut rooms, and use them only in their cloth bag, which Zippo says stops them overheating (Zippo hand warmer guide). The council says the case can pass 70 °C and the top reach 100 °C, and too much fluid leaks and is a fire risk, so fill to the line and wipe off any excess before lighting (HK Consumer Council, Zippo hand warmer). To pause one, seal out the air: Ignik says its part-used packs kept in their airtight pouch can be used again up to 72 hours later (Ignik reuse). Useless for warmth: instant cold packs.
